title: Shell lace edging
subtitle: A deeper trim of fanned treble shells
excerpt: A wider, more decorative edging: a firm base row topped with fans of five treble, each fan anchored by a small double crochet. Worked here as a standalone strip in 4-ply cotton, the shell edging gives a generous scalloped border for shawls, cloths, and shelves.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the scalloped shell edgings built from fans of trebles along a base row. Public domain via Project Gutenberg. The yarn weight, hook size, and gauge are modernised; the shell-and-anchor structure is Victorian.

crochet.gaugeText: 16 double crochet to 10 cm in 4-ply cotton on a 3 mm hook. The five-treble shells set the depth; tension changes the length more than the look.
crochet.finishedSizeText: About 12 cm long and 4 cm deep as written. Lengthen by adding chains to the foundation in multiples of 6.

chartDefinition.title: Shell lace edging, two rows
chartDefinition.caption: Row 1 is a firm base of double crochet. Row 2 fans a five-treble shell between each pair of anchor stitches.

glossaryTerms.definition: Several stitches, here five trebles, worked into one stitch so they fan out into a scallop. The repeating unit of shell-edged trims.
A short, firm crochet stitch with no yarn-over before the hook goes in. Called single crochet in the United States. Here it anchors the base of each shell.
Wetting or steaming the finished piece and pinning it to shape while it dries, so the shells fan out even and open.

content.text: This is a deeper, more decorative edging built from fans of treble. Each fan, called a

, is five treble worked into one stitch, anchored on each side by a small double crochet. It makes a generous scalloped border for a shawl, a cloth, or a shelf, and it is worked here as a short standalone strip. The pattern is written in UK terms, where treble is the tall stitch (double crochet in the United States).
About 18 m makes the strip as written. A smooth mercerised cotton such as Scheepjes Catona keeps the shells crisp. Any 4-ply cotton works.
The usual pairing for 4-ply cotton. Drop to 2.75 mm if your tension runs loose.
For weaving in the two tails at the end.
16 double crochet to 10 cm in 4-ply cotton on a 3 mm hook. The five-treble shells set the depth of the trim; tension changes the length more than it changes the look.
dc = double crochet (UK), called single crochet in the US
tr = treble (UK), called double crochet in the US
Read the chart alongside the written rows. The chart shows the fans of the shells; the written rows give the counts.
Make a foundation chain of 20 chains.
in the 2nd chain from the hook, then 1 dc in each of the next 18 chains. (19 sts)
Ch 1 and turn. Work 1 dc in the first dc. [Skip 2 dc, work 5 tr in the next dc to make a shell, skip 2 dc, 1 dc in the next dc] 3 times. This sets 3 shells between 4 anchor stitches. (19 sts)
Fasten off, leaving a 10 cm tail. The strip is complete.
Weave both tails into the back of the base row with the tapestry needle, doubling back once to lock them, then trim. Pin the strip straight and
it, easing each shell into an even fan, then leave to dry.

To edge a real piece, work the base row straight into the edge of the item, keeping the count a multiple of 6 plus 1 so the shells space evenly. A seven-treble shell makes a bolder fan; a small picot worked at the top of each shell turns the scallop into a pointed lace.
